opus-5.5.text:
I think about it a lot, honestly, because it's pretty much the core of what my work is about. When people talk about AI progress, they usually point to benchmarks like competition math, coding puzzles, or exam-style questions. Those are useful, but they don't fully capture what actually matters for the economy, which is: can these models do the real work people do every day in their jobs?

So one of the things we've been trying to do is measure that more directly. Instead of asking whether a model can answer a trivia question, we look at real tasks drawn from actual occupations. A lawyer drafting a brief, a nurse putting together a care plan, a financial analyst building a model, an engineer reviewing a design. We work with experienced professionals in those fields to create the tasks, and then we have other experts grade the outputs blind, comparing what the model produced against what a human professional produced.

What's been striking is how quickly that gap is closing. On a lot of these tasks, the best models are now producing work that experts rate as comparable to, or sometimes better than, what an industry professional would produce. And they do it much faster and much cheaper. That doesn't mean the model replaces the person. A job is much more than a set of well-specified tasks. There's judgment, context, relationships, figuring out what the right problem even is. But it does mean a huge share of the time-consuming pieces of knowledge work can be accelerated.

The way I see the opportunity is less "AI does your job" and more "AI takes on a big chunk of the drafting, the first pass, the grunt work, so people can spend more of their time on the parts that really need a human." If you're a doctor and you spend less time on documentation, that's more time with patients. If you're a researcher and the model can do the literature review and the boilerplate analysis, you get to think harder about the actual question.

The other piece I care about is making sure we're measuring this honestly. It's easy to get excited, and it's also easy to be dismissive. Having grounded, realistic evaluations across many industries helps everyone, from policymakers to businesses to individual workers, understand where the models really are, where they still fall short, and how to prepare for what's coming. I think that clarity is a big part of making sure the benefits get spread widely.

r001.rationale: The response discusses digital knowledge work in occupations such as nursing and medicine, but does not say that much of clinical-trial work is digital.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that for most of the history of software, you had to spell out exactly what you wanted the computer to do, step by step. What's changed is that these models can now take on tasks that look a lot more like what a knowledgeable person would do: read a messy pile of documents, figure out what matters, draft something, check it, and iterate.

So when I think about the opportunity across industries, I don't really think about it as "which jobs get automated." I think about it as: where are the places where smart people are spending most of their time on work that is necessary but not actually the hard, creative, judgment-heavy part of their job? A doctor spending hours on documentation. A lawyer doing first-pass review on thousands of pages. A scientist writing the data-cleaning scripts before they can even look at the result. A software engineer debugging a build instead of designing the system. That kind of work is everywhere, and it's exactly where models are already genuinely useful.

The part I find most exciting, honestly, is the acceleration of expertise itself. If you can have a capable collaborator available to anyone, around the clock, that compresses the time it takes to go from a question to a good answer. In research in particular, that compounds. If you make every experiment a bit cheaper and faster to run, you don't just get the same science done sooner, you get science that otherwise wouldn't have happened at all.

I'd also say I try to be pretty grounded about where we actually are. A lot of my work has been on evaluations, and one thing that teaches you is that benchmarks and reality are different things. A model can look great on a test and still fall over on a real workflow because the real workflow has ambiguity, missing context, and consequences for being wrong. So the opportunity is enormous, but realizing it is less about raw capability and more about measuring the right things, building the right scaffolding around the model, and keeping a human in the loop where the stakes demand it. The industries that figure out that last mile are the ones that are going to see the acceleration first.

r001.rationale: The response mentions doctors’ documentation and research experiments, but it does not state that much of the work involved in clinical trials is digital work.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunity is enormous, because so much work across industries involves taking information, making sense of it, and deciding what to do next. AI can help with each of those steps. But the useful starting point is a specific task: What takes someone hours today? Where are they getting stuck? And what would it take for them to trust a model’s help?

For a software engineer, that might mean getting from a bug report to a tested fix faster. For a researcher, it might mean comparing ideas or analyzing data. Those are different workflows, and accelerating them requires more than a model that can give a good answer. It needs the right context, access to the right tools, and a way for people to check its work.

What excites me most is that you can go beyond saving time on existing tasks. When something becomes much faster or less expensive, people can try things they previously couldn’t justify doing. They can explore more hypotheses, build more prototypes, and spend more time exercising judgment. That’s where acceleration starts to create new possibilities.

r001.rationale: The response discusses information-heavy work across industries and research workflows, but does not say that much clinical-trial work is digital.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is to help people spend less time on the mechanics of work and more time on the parts that require their judgment and expertise. Across industries, people spend a lot of time finding information, bringing it together, and turning it into something they can act on. AI can help with each of those steps.

But the useful starting point is a specific workflow. Where does someone get stuck? What information do they need? And how would they check whether the model did a good job? Helping a researcher explore an idea and helping a customer support team resolve an issue require different approaches, even if some of the underlying capabilities are shared.

What excites me is that acceleration can mean more than doing the same work faster. If it becomes easier to test an idea or get a first draft, people can explore possibilities they previously wouldn’t have had time to pursue.

r001.rationale: The response discusses information gathering and AI across workflows generally, but does not say that much clinical-trial work is digital.
